ECHO: Learning Epistemically Adaptive Language Agents with Turn-Level Credit

Abhijnan Nath ††thanks: Work done while at Colorado State University.    Nikhil Krishnaswamy Affiliation: Situated Grounding and Natural Language (SIGNAL) Lab Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Colorado State University Affiliation: Fort Collins, CO 80523 USA Email: {abhijnan.nath,nkrishna}@colostate.edu
Abstract

What does it mean for a language agent to be adaptive? Effective multi-turn agents must decide what information to seek, how to use new evidence, and when they are certain enough to act. We introduce Epistemic Decision Processes (EDPs), a belief-state formulation of multi-turn information seeking in which actions produce external observations that update the agent’s posterior over a latent task variable. EDPs make epistemic adaptivity explicit: good policies choose actions that are useful under the current belief, not merely those that correlate with eventual success. We prove that belief-agnostic policies can suffer errors that compound exponentially over the horizon, and that aggregate trajectory returns can fail to identify the per-turn Bayesian advantage needed for epistemic credit. We then introduce ECHO (Epistemic Credit for History-Conditioned Optimization), a practical clipped policy-gradient objective that assigns turn-level credit using posterior-sensitive rewards. In the Clue Selector Game, a novel controlled evidence-seeking benchmark, we show that ECHO substantially improves resolution, information gain, and efficiency over trajectory-level GRPO, and matches or exceeds frontier baselines on epistemic metrics such as grounding, recovery, and calibration while producing almost no visible reasoning text. Code and data: https://github.com/csu-signal/echo-edp

1 Introduction

In multi-step problem solving, including medical diagnoses, technical troubleshooting, scientific inquiry, and search, effective agents must decide what evidence to gather next; they do not merely act upon incomplete information [23, 47, 48, 56]. This skill is central to human learning and question asking [12, 19, 41, 50], and increasingly so to LLM agents that search the web [13, 67, 75], call tools [53], inspect documents [71], and revise actions as observations arrive [18, 68]. In such settings, the value of an information-seeking question depends on the current belief state: what is already known, what uncertainty remains, and whether the answer would change future action [30]. Thus, adaptivity is fundamentally epistemic [41, 50]—good agents choose actions that reduce not just global uncertainty, but the uncertainty that matters most in the current context.

In multi-turn tasks, final success may only be known at the end of the trajectory. Intermediate rewards are often unavailable, learned approximately through process reward models [11, 24, 35], or disconnected from whether a query actually changed the agent’s belief (e.g., when rewarding only task outcomes). The agent’s uncertainty is often organized around a hidden variable of interest, such as a goal or sub-goal, that must be inferred through interaction rather than revealed directly [1, 40, 72, 73]. While the agent may observe the full history of its own queries and the resulting feedback, the value of the next action still depends on how that history changes its belief. This creates a credit-assignment problem that existing methods do not fully address [8, 34, 46].

We argue that information-seeking agents need more than temporal credit assignment for optimal behavior: they need epistemic credit assignment, which reflects the usefulness of evidence elicited by an action given the agent’s current belief, not merely that it appears in a trajectory that eventually succeeds. We formalize this through Epistemic Decision Processes (EDPs), a belief-state view11 1 EDPs are a task-level specialization of belief-state decision processes: unlike BAMDPs [15, 39], which typically model uncertainty over transition/reward parameters or latent MDP identities, EDPs focus on uncertainty over a hidden task variable under a fixed interaction interface; see Sec. 3 and Appendix A for details. of multi-turn information seeking in which actions produce external observations that update a posterior over a latent task variable. Our theory shows why this distinction matters: there exist long-horizon information-seeking tasks where belief-sensitive policies are necessary for strong performance, while trajectory-level returns can be too coarse to identify which turns actually reduced uncertainty.

We then introduce ECHO, a clipped policy-gradient objective that assigns turn-level credit using posterior-sensitive rewards. ECHO trains agents to ask questions that are useful under the current belief state, not merely questions that correlate with eventual success. We instantiate this setting in the Clue Selector Game (CSG), a deduction task where the hypothesis space, candidate posterior, and belief updates are exactly measurable. Inspired by prior work in step-level epistemic competence [58], CSG evaluates both final resolution and process-level epistemic behavior, using diagnostics such as groundedness, zero-information turns, recovery after low-information actions, and late-stage calibration. Empirically, ECHO trains a 1.5B policy to reach frontier-level task resolution, reduce zero-elimination turns, and learn substantially faster than standard RL methods, while producing almost no visible reasoning text. This reveals a form of “silent exploration”: adaptive information seeking expressed through belief-conditioned actions rather than long chains of thought.

Our novel contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce Epistemic Decision Processes (EDPs), a belief-state formulation of multi-turn information-seeking language agents, and define epistemic adaptivity as posterior-sensitive action selection.

  2. 2.

    We prove that belief-sensitive policies are necessary for strong performance in EDPs, with an exponential gap over belief-agnostic policies, and that aggregate trajectory return is generally insufficient for recovering per-turn Bayesian advantage.

  3. 3.

    We introduce ECHO, a clipped policy-gradient objective for epistemic credit assignment over posterior-sensitive turn rewards, and evaluate it in the Clue Selector Game, a controlled EDP benchmark with explicit beliefs and measurable posterior contraction. ECHO outperforms trajectory-level GRPO and prompting baselines in resolution, information gain, and sample efficiency, while showing strong grounding, recovery, and calibration with little visible reasoning.

2 Related Work

Temporal credit assignment and in-context learning

Standard temporal credit assignment [6, 55, 59, 64] can propagate delayed rewards to earlier turns in a task, but unless the state or reward explicitly represents belief change, it does not identify whether an action reduced uncertainty under the belief state at that moment. LLM agents’ full query–observation history can be placed in-context [9, 43]; the model could, in principle, update its belief in-context and ask the next informative question. However, recent work suggests that in-context updating is sensitive to attention biases, context-length, and implicit priors shaped by pretraining [33, 37, 17]. Bayesian methods such as BED-LLM compute informative queries at inference time using expected information gain over the variable of interest [10, 16, 24, 40, 72]. However, these methods also highlight why belief-sensitive learning is difficult in realistic language tasks: the hypothesis space’s pretraining and implicit priors make the agent’s posterior difficult to inspect or credit at each step. Moreover, inference-time strategies [27, 68] must recompute query utility at every turn; they do not bake in adaptive querying to the policy.

Bayesian learning and belief-conditioned policies

Epistemic adaptivity builds on belief-conditioned decision making: agents represent uncertainty, update it from evidence, and act to make future decisions better informed. Bayes-Adaptive MDPs formalize this by augmenting state with a posterior over environment parameters or latent MDP identities [7, 15, 20], with deep RL extensions using approximate inference [77]. Language-based information seeking also requires crediting actions for changing belief; otherwise, outcome-based RL can lock agents into low-information interaction patterns [78]. Training-time Bayes-adaptive methods such as BARL encourage reflective exploration within generated reasoning traces [70], but recent work cautions that visible reasoning traces are not necessarily faithful evidence of reasoning competence [45, 51]. ECHO via EDPs instead studies “silent exploration” across external query–observation turns in a multiturn setup, where adaptivity is expressed through belief-informative actions rather than verbalized rationales.

Controlled environments for information-seeking agents

Common question-asking settings—including entity deduction, 20-questions-style tasks, active task disambiguation, and preference elicitation—study how agents infer hidden targets through interaction [3, 32, 36, 72, 76]. However, non-uniform LLM priors affect question selection and evaluation [40]; intermediate progress is usually tracked via hand-crafted knowledge-bases [74] or approximated through learned reward networks, process reward models, or inference-time information-gain estimates [10, 11, 24, 35]. Final accuracy can miss process-level failures such as information self-locking, poor grounding, or failure to recognize knowledge gaps [58, 78]. Web-search, tool-use, and embodied environments expose richer interactions [5, 25, 28, 49, 61], but their complexity can obscure which action improved the agent’s knowledge state. Our Clue Selector Game (CSG) is a controlled complement: it preserves a language-mediated multi-turn loop—action, response, belief update, and subsequent action—while making the hypothesis space explicit, the posterior exactly measurable, and process-level metrics such as grounding, redundancy, zero-information behavior, recovery, and calibration directly computable.

3 Epistemic Decision Processes

We now formalize multi-turn information seeking as a decision problem over beliefs. An agent acts under uncertainty about a latent task variable z⋆z^{\star}, chooses actions that elicit external observations, and updates its belief from those observations before choosing the next action. The key EDP property is that the main dense reward is posterior-sensitive: the same question can be useful under one candidate set and uninformative under another.

This differs from single-response reasoning settings, where adaptation occurs primarily within a generated trace before feedback is received [70]. In an EDP, the policy interacts with an external environment over multiple turns: each action produces an observation, the observation changes the posterior, and the next action should be chosen under the updated belief [1]. Intuitively, optimal policies in this setting are epistemically adaptive: they choose actions because they are useful under the current belief, not merely because they are plausible given the observable surface history.

We formalize this as an Epistemic Decision Process (EDP), a finite-horizon interaction defined by:

ℰ=(𝒵,ρ0,𝒜,Ω,O,u,T).\mathcal{E}=\left(\mathcal{Z},\rho_{0},\mathcal{A},\Omega,O,u,T\right).

Here, z⋆∈𝒵z^{\star}\in\mathcal{Z} denotes the latent task variable sampled from prior ρ0\rho_{0}—for example, a target hypothesis, user intent, diagnosis, or answer state—while 𝒜\mathcal{A}, Ω\Omega, OO, uu, and TT denote the action space, observation space, observation kernel, evidential utility, and horizon. At turn tt, the interaction history ht=(a0,o0,…,at−1,ot−1)h_{t}=(a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) induces a posterior belief bt​(z):=ℙ⁡(z⋆=z∣ht)b_{t}(z):=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}=z\mid h_{t}).22 2 In LLM implementations, the serialized prompt may include a textual state summary, such as remaining hypotheses. We treat this as an encoding of the epistemic component btb_{t}. The agent samples an action at∼πθ(⋅∣ht)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}), receives an external observation ot∼O(⋅∣z⋆,ht,at)o_{t}\sim O(\cdot\mid z^{\star},h_{t},a_{t}), and updates its posterior via a Bayesian belief-update operator bt+1=τ⁡(bt,ht,at,ot)b_{t+1}=\tau(b_{t},h_{t},a_{t},o_{t}), where τ\tau is induced by OO. Fig. 2 shows a conceptualization of the EDP.

LLM Instantiation

The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is an autoregressive LLM that gets a serialized history hth_{t}, including the task instruction, current state summary, and previous action–observation pairs. The model generates a structured output that is parsed as the action ata_{t}, such as a query or information-seeking move. The observation oto_{t} from the environment is used to update the environment state by filtering the hypotheses still consistent with the evidence. Thus, the transition is not merely deterministic text concatenation [52]: although the next prompt appends (at,ot)(a_{t},o_{t}), the observation itself is produced by an external kernel ot∼O(⋅∣z⋆,ht,at)o_{t}\sim O(\cdot\mid z^{\star},h_{t},a_{t}). Each turn is therefore a genuine environment interaction, and the decision-relevant state is the posterior uncertainty induced by the history, i.e., the augmented epistemic state (s⁡(ht),bt,t)(s(h_{t}),b_{t},t), rather than only the visible text or turn index.

Bayesian Value and Advantage

To train an epistemically adaptive policy (Fig. 2), we need a credit signal that evaluates actions under the agent’s current posterior belief, rather than only under the final episode outcome. For a fixed latent task zz, let Qzπ(ht,at)=𝔼π,O[∑s=tT−1u(bs,as,os)+RT(hT,z)∣ht,at,z⋆=z]Q_{z}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,O}[\sum_{s=t}^{T-1}u(b_{s},a_{s},o_{s})+R_{T}(h_{T},z)\mid h_{t},a_{t},z^{\star}=z] denote the value of taking action ata_{t} after history hth_{t}, where RTR_{T} is any terminal task reward. Since the agent does not observe z⋆z^{\star}, the relevant value is posterior-weighted: QBπ​(ht,at)=𝔼z∼bt​[Qzπ​(ht,at)]Q_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim b_{t}}[Q_{z}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t})]. The corresponding Bayesian advantage is ABπ(ht,at)=QBπ(ht,at)−𝔼a′∼π(⋅∣ht)[QBπ(ht,a′)]A_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t})=Q_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t})-\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t})}[Q_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a^{\prime})]. Since bt=b⁡(ht)b_{t}=b(h_{t}), the dependence on the current belief is implicit in the history argument; equivalently, ABπ​(ht,at)A_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t}) evaluates the action under the posterior induced by hth_{t}. Intuitively, this asks whether ata_{t} is better than alternative actions available under the same posterior belief. At first glance, estimating this quantity exactly would require branching multiple actions from the same history hth_{t}, which is expensive in multi-turn interactive environments for LLMs [1, 22, 31, 70]. This raises two crucial questions: what policy class is this Bayesian advantage meant to favor, and how can we approximate its credit signal without exhaustive same-history branching? We first answer the policy question by distinguishing belief-agnostic policies from epistemically adaptive ones; we then introduce a tractable Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator that uses turn-level epistemic rewards as a practical surrogate for the belief-conditioned advantage.

3.1 Distinguishing Epistemically Adaptive from Belief-Agnostic Policies

An epistemically adaptive policy uses the belief induced by the interaction history, not just the history itself. Let s⁡(ht)s(h_{t}) denote the belief-independent task context, as shown in Fig. 2. These variables constrain what the agent can do at turn tt, but do not themselves encode the posterior over z⋆z^{\star}. A policy is belief-agnostic if its dependence on history factors only through this interface state, i.e., there exists a decision rule gg such that π⁡(at∣ht)=g⁡(at∣s⁡(ht))\pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=g(a_{t}\mid s(h_{t})). In contrast, a policy is epistemically adaptive if its action distribution can also depend on the posterior belief induced by the history, i.e., there exists a decision rule ff such that π⁡(at∣ht)=f⁡(at∣s⁡(ht),bt)\pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=f(a_{t}\mid s(h_{t}),b_{t}). We say the policy is strictly epistemically adaptive if there exist histories ht,ht′h_{t},h^{\prime}_{t} with the same interface state s⁡(ht)=s⁡(ht′)s(h_{t})=s(h^{\prime}_{t}) but different beliefs bt≠bt′b_{t}\neq b^{\prime}_{t}, such that π(⋅∣ht)≠π(⋅∣ht′)\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t})\neq\pi(\cdot\mid h^{\prime}_{t}).

Remark on Proposition 3.1

Once the belief btb_{t} is part of the state, optimal behavior can be written as a Markov policy over (s⁡(ht),bt,t)(s(h_{t}),b_{t},t). The important question is therefore not whether a Markov policy exists, but whether the training signal can teach the policy to use the belief as uncertainty is resolved [70]. In long-horizon information-seeking tasks, this is a depth-wise credit-assignment problem: at each turn, the useful action depends on the current posterior, and failing to adapt even once can derail the remaining trajectory. The first part of Theorem 3.2 makes this sharp: there are EDPs where an adaptive policy succeeds with probability 11, while any belief-agnostic policy succeeds with probability at most 21−d2^{1-d}, decaying exponentially with horizon. The second part of Theorem 3.2 then shows why sparse trajectory-level returns are a poor learning signal for this behavior: they reveal final success, but not the belief-conditioned credit of each intermediate action. Together, these results motivate turn-level epistemic credit rather than trajectory-level credit.

4 Depth-wise Epistemic Credit Optimization (ECHO)

Theorem 3.2 shows that aggregate trajectory return can alias belief-distinct decisions. More generally, two trajectories can have the same final reward while containing very different intermediate evidence-gathering behavior, so total return alone cannot identify which actions reduced uncertainty. This leads to our core insight—actions should receive credit based on whether they were useful under the belief state in which they were chosen, not only based on whether the entire episode eventually succeeded. We therefore introduce ECHO (Epistemic Credit for History-Conditioned Optimization), a practical turn-level surrogate for Bayesian advantage in multi-turn EDPs. Like GRPO [59], ECHO uses group-normalized advantages and a clipped policy-gradient objective [55]; unlike trajectory-level GRPO, it normalizes posterior-sensitive turn rewards rather than full episode returns. As such, ECHO keeps the practical group-relative clipped optimization form of GRPO, but shifts the credit signal from trajectory-level success to turn-level “epistemic” progress.

Specifically, for each training instance, we sample GG parallel rollouts from the old policy. At turn tt, rollout gg has history ht(g)h_{t}^{(g)}, belief bt(g)=ℙ⁡(z⋆∣ht(g))b_{t}^{(g)}=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}\mid h_{t}^{(g)}), sampled action at(g)∼πθold(⋅∣ht(g))a_{t}^{(g)}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid h_{t}^{(g)}), and external observation ot(g)o_{t}^{(g)}. We assign a posterior-sensitive turn reward:

rt(g)=u⁡(bt(g),at(g),ot(g)),r_{t}^{(g)}=u\!\left(b_{t}^{(g)},a_{t}^{(g)},o_{t}^{(g)}\right),

which measures local epistemic progress, such as information gain, reduction in posterior uncertainty, or elimination of inconsistent hypotheses. Sec. 5.1 shows how this reward design fits into an EDP environment. At each decision depth tt, we normalize these rewards across the active rollouts:

A^t(g),ECHO=rt(g)−1|𝒢t|​∑j∈𝒢trt(j)stdj∈𝒢t⁡(rt(j))+ϵ\widehat{A}_{t}^{(g),\mathrm{ECHO}}=\frac{r_{t}^{(g)}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{t}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}r_{t}^{(j)}}{\operatorname{std}_{j\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}(r_{t}^{(j)})+\epsilon} (1)

Unlike trajectory-level GRPO, which broadcasts a single full-episode advantage across all actions in a rollout, ECHO—as shown in Eq. 1—computes group-normalized advantages at each decision depth. This gives each structured turn action credit according to the epistemic progress it produced under the current posterior [29, 42, 52]. We note that our approach is not an exact belief-local advantage after rollouts diverge, since different rollouts may reach different histories and beliefs at the same turn—given the exponential state-action spaces in language based RL using LLMs [14, 62, 76]. The key point that each reward is evaluated relative to its rollout’s own posterior, so the update preserves belief-dependent variation in action quality while avoiding exhaustive same-history branching. 5 Experiments

5.1 Clue Selector Game Environment as an EDP

We instantiate EDPs through the Clue Selector Game (CSG), a controlled multi-turn information-seeking task inspired by prior work in multiturn RL [1]. In the CSG, the agent must identify a hidden secret number by sequentially querying a clue-holder oracle that knows the secret but is not allowed to reveal it directly. Instead, the oracle can only answer property-based questions about the secret. To make the action space structured33 3 The action space is still diverse due to the query component, which admits open-ended question generation., the agent acts through an arm–question interface: at each turn it routes a natural-language property question through one of several clue-holder arms, where each arm “owns” certain domains of information. This setup lets us test whether a policy can do more than ask plausible questions in isolation: under the current candidate set, a successful agent identifies what information is most useful to seek (the arm), avoids repeatedly asking for information already obtained, and adapts its query strategy as its belief over the secret changes. The arms therefore provide a lightweight yet explicit scaffolding to examine the adaptivity of the query strategy. Figs. 3 and 6 show a high-level overview of the CSG environment and the prompts used, respectively.

Game dynamics

A secret integer n⋆∈{1,…,N}n^{\star}\in\{1,\ldots,N\} is sampled uniformly at random; we use N=100N=100 for training, while evaluation can include secrets up to N=200N=200 to test generalization. At each turn, the agent poses a natural-language property question to a fixed oracle that answers truthfully without revealing the secret. The action space pairs each question with a categorical arm label that groups questions by property family (e.g., parity, divisibility, range); this provides lightweight structure over the action space (see above) but does not affect the oracle’s response. The dominant reward is posterior-sensitive candidate elimination; a small shaping bonus for arm–question consistency is included but is not the focus of our analysis.

CSG’s explicit EDP interpretation

The latent task variable is the secret number z⋆=n⋆z^{\star}=n^{\star}. The history hth_{t} consists of the previous arm selections, questions, and oracle observations. The belief state btb_{t} is the posterior over the secret number induced by this history. Because the secret is sampled uniformly and oracle observations only eliminate inconsistent candidates, the posterior is uniform over the remaining candidate set:

bt​(n)={1/|𝒞t|,n∈𝒞t,0,n∉𝒞t.b_{t}(n)=\begin{cases}1/|\mathcal{C}_{t}|,&n\in\mathcal{C}_{t},\\ 0,&n\notin\mathcal{C}_{t}.\end{cases}

For example, if the initial candidates are {1,…,10}\{1,\ldots,10\} and the agent asks whether the number is even, a truthful “yes” response updates the candidate set to {2,4,6,8,10}\{2,4,6,8,10\}, making the posterior uniform over those five numbers. Thus, in CSG, the candidate set is not merely a textual state variable; it is a direct representation of the agent’s epistemic state.

Turn-level utility measures epistemic progress. The dominant reward term is fractional candidate elimination, rinfo=(|𝒞t|−|𝒞t+1|)/|𝒞t|r_{\mathrm{info}}=(|\mathcal{C}_{t}|-|\mathcal{C}_{t+1}|)/|\mathcal{C}_{t}|, which measures how much the action contracts the current posterior. Training also includes small shaping terms for valid arm–question matching and query diversity, a redundancy penalty for repetition, and sparse bonuses for resolving the task efficiently. The action value is therefore belief-dependent: two histories may share the same belief-independent task context—for example, the same turn index, action schema, and remaining budget—while inducing different posteriors over z⋆z^{\star}, and therefore requiring different useful actions. The posterior-sensitive reward signal is used by ECHO and other RL baselines for training; it assigns credit based on the epistemic progress made at the turn where the action was chosen, rather than broadcasting only the final episode outcome. CSG is therefore a clean testbed for our theory.

Evaluation Strategy

Our metrics test whether a policy uses accumulated evidence to choose useful actions throughout the trajectory, rather than merely succeeding at the end or producing more reasoning text. In CSG, optimal information seeking is not determined by turn number alone, but by the structure of the current posterior over candidates, i.e., the specific composition of the surviving candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}. An epistemically adaptive agent should therefore ask questions that reduce uncertainty under the current 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, avoid redundant queries, recover after low-information observations, and not ask broad questions if the belief state is narrow. Accordingly, we evaluate not only final task resolution, but also process-level epistemic quality [58] as a proxy for epistemic adaptability (see Sec. 6). We report Zero, the rate of non-redundant turns that eliminate no candidates; Qual., the candidate-elimination quality normalized by an ideal split; and Ground, the rate of turns that are both non-redundant and informative under the current candidate set. To measure robustness after local epistemic failures, we also report GRecover, the rate at which the next turn after a zero-elimination action is grounded as defined above, and ResAfterZero, the fraction of episodes that still resolve after at least one zero-elimination event. Finally, Reason% measures explicit reasoning text outside the required action format. Further details on evaluation metrics are provided in Appendix C.1.

Empirically, these metrics are strongly tied to task success: across evaluation episodes, resolution correlates positively with elimination quality and groundedness, and negatively with zero-elimination and low-information behavior, supporting their use as indicators of epistemically adaptive behavior.

Baselines

Frontier or proprietary models include Claude Sonnet 4.6, OpenAI’s o3-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, and GPT-4o-mini, evaluated zero-shot with the standard task prompt. These models represent strong off-the-shelf performance without task-specific training. Prompting variants evaluate Qwen2.5-1.5B Instruct with explicit reasoning prompts: chain-of-thought (CoT), full ReAct [68] using a complete Thought/Action/Observation loop with growing history context, and a simple version of ReAct using a Thought/Action format in the system prompt. These baselines test whether eliciting explicit reasoning can substitute for RL training on the same base model. We also include GPT-4o w/ full ReAct, which tests whether a structured reasoning loop improves a capable frontier model. RL baselines are trained on Qwen2.5-1.5B Instruct using the same environment and reward function as ECHO, differing only in the advantage estimator. The main RL baseline is episode-return RL, which broadcasts the total episode reward uniformly to all turns (and thereby, to tokens) consistent with the standard GRPO formulation when extended to multi-turn settings; we also include RLOO [2] per-turn to isolate the effect of per-turn relative credit. Offline SFT+RL is a single-turn offline baseline trained from pre-collected trajectories, representing training on fixed demonstrations rather than online interaction. Base Qwen 2.5 at sizes from 0.5B–14B provide a scaling reference without task-specific prompting or RL. Finally, a greedy oracle reference policy with access to the secret during action selection, that chooses the arm-question pair with maximal candidate elimination, serves as an “upper-bound” [66] diagnostic.

6 Results

ECHO improves both resolution and epistemic behavior.

Table 1 shows that ECHO achieves the strongest learned-policy performance in CSG. Its resolve rate of 45.3%45.3\% exceeds the best frontier baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.6 (43.1%43.1\%), and substantially outperforms episodic-return GRPO (14.7%14.7\%), RLOO per-turn (13.8%13.8\%), and all base/prompting baselines. More importantly, the improvement is reflected in process-level epistemic behavior: ECHO has the lowest zero-elimination rate (18.6%18.6\%), indicating that its questions most often update the agent belief state. While Claude attains slightly higher per-turn quality and groundedness, ECHO combines high elimination quality (0.6700.670) and groundedness (0.7180.718) with much stronger trajectory-level robustness: after zero-elimination events, it has the highest grounded recovery (0.4060.406) and resolution-after-zero rate (0.3180.318). This suggests that ECHO’s advantage is not merely asking strong individual questions, but that the ECHO-trained policy learns more robust information-gathering behavior across the trajectory: it asks well-grounded questions, avoids zero-elimination actions, and recovers when a local epistemic failure occurs. ECHO also achieves these gains with almost no explicit reasoning text (0.9%0.9\%) exposing its silently exploratory nature, whereas ReAct variants reason on every turn but do not improve resolution, indicating that explicit reasoning traces alone do not substitute for epistemically adaptive training. Arm-level diagnostics further show that ECHO’s arm–question choices remain informative even under same-arm reuse, suggesting belief-conditioned routing rather than superficial arm switching (full results in Table 5 in Appendix C). Additional results are reported in Appendix B and C.

Behavioral diagnostics reveal why ECHO succeeds.

To understand whether ECHO’s gains come from genuine belief-state adaptation, we analyze process-level diagnostics across policies in Fig. 4. Results show that resolution is tightly linked to posterior contraction: models with fewer zero-elimination turns and higher elimination quality achieve higher solve rates, with ECHO occupying the favorable region of high resolution and low wasted updates. Fig. 4(c) further shows that ECHO continues shrinking the candidate set across turns, whereas episodic-return GRPO and prompting baselines flatten earlier, indicating stalled information acquisition. Fig. 4(d) shows that ECHO is more robust after local epistemic failures: following zero-elimination events, it produces more grounded recoveries and is substantially more likely to still resolve the episode. Together, these diagnostics support the central mechanism behind ECHO: it learns to ask questions that remain informative under the evolving belief state, rather than being merely plausible.

What epistemically adaptive behavior looks like.

The qualitative trajectory in Fig. 3 illustrates the same mechanism at the episode level. For the same secret, ECHO asks questions that remain useful under the changing candidate set, progressively contracting the belief state until only the target remains, while episodic-return GRPO asks questions that are initially plausible, but then non-informative, producing several zero-elimination turns. Thus, the failure mode is stale information seeking: otherwise reasonable questions that are no longer informative after earlier observations.

Explicit reasoning does not substitute for epistemic training.

Explicit reasoning traces alone do not produce epistemic adaptability in long-horizon EDPs. Full ReAct forces models to reason on nearly every turn, yet GPT-4o + Full ReAct resolves only 25.3%25.3\% of episodes. Qwen2.5-1.5B + Full ReAct resolves only 4.4%4.4\%. By contrast, ECHO resolves 45.3%45.3\% of episodes and produces explicit reasoning text on only 0.9%0.9\% of turns. This suggests that the central bottleneck for epistemic adaptivity is not verbalizing intermediate reasoning, but learning a policy conditioned on the evolving belief state. This is “silent exploration” (Sec. 3) manifest: adaptive information seeking expressed through query choices and posterior-sensitive feedback rather than long test-time reasoning traces. ECHO trains adaptable models using belief-sensitive reward structures and provides strong performance with higher token cost-efficiency—a trend consistent with prior works [38] in LLM reasoning.

Training dynamics support turn-level epistemic credit assignment.

Fig. 5 shows that ECHO’s gains emerge as a turn-level epistemic learning effect rather than as a generic reward increase. By the end of training, ECHO reaches much higher episode resolution than trajectory-level GRPO (70.1%70.1\% vs. 15.9%15.9\%), eliminates more candidates per turn (13.0413.04 vs. 10.3310.33), and reduces redundancy almost completely (0.2%0.2\% vs. 2.5%2.5\%). It also resolves more often at the turn level (9.3%9.3\% vs. 1.8%1.8\%) and shortens average episodes (7.677.67 vs. 9.299.29 turns). These trends match our theoretical analysis of EDPs (Sec. 3): when credit is assigned at the decision depth where an action changes the posterior, the policy learns to ask questions that contract the current candidate set rather than merely optimize a sparse final outcome in a multiturn task. The optimization diagnostics suggest specialization rather than mode collapse [26, 69]: ECHO’s entropy decreases while query diversity remains near saturation, indicating that the policy becomes more selective without repeating the same questions. In contrast, GRPO maintains higher entropy but achieves lower information gain and far lower resolution, consistent with trajectory-level credit failing to identify which intermediate actions were useful under the current belief. Overall, these results indicate that aggregate trajectory returns can fail to identify the per-turn Bayesian advantage needed for epistemic credit.

7 Conclusion

We introduced Epistemic Decision Processes (EDPs), a belief-state formulation of multi-turn information seeking, and showed theoretically why trajectory-level success is insufficient for epistemic credit assignment: policies must receive credit at the decision points where actions change the posterior. Building on this view, we proposed ECHO, a turn-level optimization framework that rewards posterior-sensitive information gain and trains policies to be epistemically adaptive. In the Clue Selector Game, ECHO trains a 1.5B policy that exceeds strong proprietary frontier baselines such as Claude Sonnet 4.6 and reasoning-observation focused baselines like ReAct on final task resolution, while also reducing zero-elimination turns, maintaining high-quality belief contraction, and recovering more robustly after local epistemic failures. These gains do not come from longer visible reasoning traces: ECHO exhibits “silent exploration,” learning adaptive information seeking through belief-conditioned actions rather than explicit rationales at inference time.

Overall, our results suggest that adaptive language agents in information-seeking long-horizon tasks should be trained and evaluated not only by whether they eventually succeed, but by how they gather evidence, update beliefs, and recover from uncertainty over time. Extending EDP-style credit assignment to richer tool-use, search, and multi-agent settings is a natural next step for future work.

Limitations

CSG provides exact Bayesian posteriors by construction (Lemma A.6), but real information-seeking tasks—medical diagnosis, web search, preference elicitation—involve implicit, high-dimensional hypothesis spaces where the belief state must be approximated [10, 11, 35], and where information sources may be noisy or adversarial. In such settings, the posterior-sensitive turn reward that drives ECHO could be challenging to compute analytically. Our experiments demonstrate ECHO at the 1.5B scale; whether epistemic credit remains necessary at larger scales where models may have stronger in-context belief tracking [33], or provides complementary gains, is an open question. Similarly, CSG operates over a relatively short horizon (e.g., 10 total turns) with a structured arm–question action space; scaling epistemic credit assignment to longer horizons with relatively open-ended actions including general-purpose tool calls and richer observation spaces [1, 28] like the web is unexplored. Extending EDPs to settings with approximate beliefs, unreliable information sources, and compositional latent structure is a natural direction for future work.

Appendix A Theory and Proofs

In this section, we provide our main theoretical results and proofs.

Proposition A.1 (Belief-state sufficiency).

Let ℰ=(𝒵,ρ0,𝒜,Ω,O,u,T)\mathcal{E}=(\mathcal{Z},\rho_{0},\mathcal{A},\Omega,O,u,T) be an Epistemic Decision Process. Let ht=(a0,o0,…,at−1,ot−1)h_{t}=(a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) denote the interaction history, and let bt​(z)=ℙ⁡(z⋆=z∣ht)b_{t}(z)=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}=z\mid h_{t}) be the posterior belief over the latent task variable. Suppose there exists a surface-state map s:ℋ→𝒮s:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{S} such that the following hold:

  1. 1.

    Observation sufficiency: the observation kernel depends on the history only through the latent variable, surface state, and action:

    O⁡(ot∣z⋆,ht,at)=O⁡(ot∣z⋆,s⁡(ht),at).O(o_{t}\mid z^{\star},h_{t},a_{t})=O(o_{t}\mid z^{\star},s(h_{t}),a_{t}).
  2. 2.

    Surface-state update sufficiency: there exists a transition map F:𝒮×𝒜×Ω→𝒮F:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathcal{S} such that

    s⁡(ht+1)=F⁡(s⁡(ht),at,ot).s(h_{t+1})=F(s(h_{t}),a_{t},o_{t}).
  3. 3.

    Utility sufficiency: the per-turn utility can be written as a measurable function of the surface state, belief, action, and observation:

    ut=u⁡(s⁡(ht),bt,at,ot).u_{t}=u(s(h_{t}),b_{t},a_{t},o_{t}).

    The terminal reward can likewise be written as RT=RT​(s⁡(hT),bT)R_{T}=R_{T}(s(h_{T}),b_{T}), or equivalently as the posterior expectation of a latent terminal reward.

Then there exists an optimal policy π⋆\pi^{\star} for the EDP that depends on the history hth_{t} only through the augmented epistemic state (s⁡(ht),bt,t)(s(h_{t}),b_{t},t).

Proof.

We prove the result by reducing the EDP to a belief-state MDP [4, 60].

Step 1: The augmented epistemic state determines future observation distributions.

Fix any history hth_{t}, action ata_{t}, surface state st=s⁡(ht)s_{t}=s(h_{t}), and belief btb_{t}. Since bt​(z)=ℙ⁡(z⋆=z∣ht)b_{t}(z)=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}=z\mid h_{t}), the predictive distribution over the next observation is

ℙ⁡(ot∣ht,at)=∫𝒵O⁡(ot∣z,st,at)​bt​(z)​𝑑z.\mathbb{P}(o_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t})=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}O(o_{t}\mid z,s_{t},a_{t})b_{t}(z)\,dz.

Thus, by the observation sufficiency assumption, the distribution of oto_{t} depends on the full history hth_{t} only through (st,bt)(s_{t},b_{t}) and the chosen action ata_{t}.

Step 2: The belief update is determined by the augmented epistemic state.

After observing oto_{t}, the posterior is updated by Bayes’ rule:

bt+1​(z)=τ⁡(bt,at,ot)​(z)=O⁡(ot∣z,st,at)​bt​(z)∫𝒵O⁡(ot∣z′,st,at)​bt​(z′)​d​z′.b_{t+1}(z)=\tau(b_{t},a_{t},o_{t})(z)=\frac{O(o_{t}\mid z,s_{t},a_{t})b_{t}(z)}{\int_{\mathcal{Z}}O(o_{t}\mid z^{\prime},s_{t},a_{t})b_{t}(z^{\prime})\,dz^{\prime}}.

Therefore, bt+1b_{t+1} is fully determined by (st,bt,at,ot)(s_{t},b_{t},a_{t},o_{t}). By the surface-state update assumption, st+1=s⁡(ht+1)=F⁡(st,at,ot)s_{t+1}=s(h_{t+1})=F(s_{t},a_{t},o_{t}). Hence the next augmented epistemic state (st+1,bt+1,t+1)(s_{t+1},b_{t+1},t+1) depends on the history only through (st,bt,t)(s_{t},b_{t},t), the action ata_{t}, and the observation oto_{t}.

Step 3: The reward is determined by the augmented epistemic state.

By the utility sufficiency assumption, the per-turn utility is u⁡(st,bt,at,ot)u(s_{t},b_{t},a_{t},o_{t}). Thus the distribution of both the next augmented state and the immediate utility is determined by (st,bt,t)(s_{t},b_{t},t) and ata_{t}. No additional information from the raw history hth_{t} is needed for predicting future rewards.

Step 4: Bellman recursion on the belief-state MDP.

Define the optimal value function on the augmented epistemic state by backward induction [63]. At the terminal step,

VT⋆​(s,b)=RT​(s,b).V_{T}^{\star}(s,b)=R_{T}(s,b).

For t<Tt<T, define

Vt⋆(s,b)=maxa∈𝒜𝔼z∼b𝔼o∼O(⋅∣z,s,a)[u(s,b,a,o)+Vt+1⋆(F(s,a,o),τ(b,a,o))].V_{t}^{\star}(s,b)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{z\sim b}\mathbb{E}_{o\sim O(\cdot\mid z,s,a)}\left[u(s,b,a,o)+V_{t+1}^{\star}(F(s,a,o),\tau(b,a,o))\right].

This Bellman recursion is well-defined because the predictive observation distribution, the belief update, the surface-state update, and the utility all depend only on (s,b,t)(s,b,t) and aa.

Step 5: Constructing an optimal policy.

For any history hth_{t}, let st=s⁡(ht)s_{t}=s(h_{t}) and bt=ℙ⁡(z⋆∣ht)b_{t}=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}\mid h_{t}). Define a greedy policy

π⋆(ht)∈argmaxa∈𝒜𝔼z∼bt𝔼o∼O(⋅∣z,st,a)[u(st,bt,a,o)+Vt+1⋆(F(st,a,o),τ(bt,a,o))].\pi^{\star}(h_{t})\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{z\sim b_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{o\sim O(\cdot\mid z,s_{t},a)}\left[u(s_{t},b_{t},a,o)+V_{t+1}^{\star}(F(s_{t},a,o),\tau(b_{t},a,o))\right].

By construction, π⋆​(ht)\pi^{\star}(h_{t}) depends on hth_{t} only through (s⁡(ht),bt,t)(s(h_{t}),b_{t},t). Moreover, by the Bellman recursion [63], this policy attains Vt⋆​(s⁡(ht),bt)V_{t}^{\star}(s(h_{t}),b_{t}) for every history hth_{t}. Therefore, π⋆\pi^{\star} is optimal, and an optimal policy exists that is Markovian [70] in the augmented epistemic state (s⁡(ht),bt,t)(s(h_{t}),b_{t},t). ∎

Significance.

Proposition A.1 justifies the EDP formulation. Although the agent observes a growing text history hth_{t}, the full history is not the fundamental decision state. What matters for optimal action selection is the visible surface state together with the posterior belief induced by the history. This separates ordinary text-state conditioning from epistemic adaptivity: a policy that ignores btb_{t} may condition on the prompt and turn index, but it cannot in general choose actions based on what the agent has learned from external observations. The result is the EDP analogue of the standard belief-MDP reduction in Bayesian RL and POMDPs, but applied to multi-turn LLM agents whose observations come from an external environment rather than from internal chain-of-thought continuation.

Connection to Bayesian RL for LLM reasoning.

This proposition parallels the belief-sufficiency argument used in Bayesian RL accounts of LLM reasoning. In BARL [70], the hidden uncertainty is over candidate MDPs or reasoning hypotheses, and the belief is updated over those hypotheses inside a generated reasoning trace. In our EDP setting, the hidden uncertainty is over an external latent task variable z⋆z^{\star}, and the belief bt​(z)=ℙ⁡(z⋆=z∣ht)b_{t}(z)=\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}=z\mid h_{t}) is updated through external observations. Thus, the proof technique is the same belief-MDP reduction, but our setting is explicitly multi-turn: the agent acts, receives evidence from the environment, updates its posterior, and then chooses the next action.

Theorem A.2 (Adaptive policies can strictly outperform belief-agnostic policies).

For every depth d≥1d\geq 1, there exists an Epistemic Decision Process ℰd\mathcal{E}_{d} with horizon dd such that:

  1. 1.

    there exists an epistemically adaptive policy π⋆\pi^{\star} with ℙ⁡(success∣π⋆)=1\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\pi^{\star})=1;

  2. 2.

    every belief-agnostic policy μ\mu satisfies ℙ⁡(success∣μ)≤21−d\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\mu)\leq 2^{1-d}.

Proof.

We construct a family of EDPs in which success requires using evidence revealed in previous turns. The construction separates policies that condition on the epistemic state from policies that do not.

Step 1: Construction of ℰd\mathcal{E}_{d}.

Let the latent task variable be a binary string z⋆=(z1⋆,…,zd⋆)∈𝒵={0,1}dz^{\star}=(z^{\star}_{1},\ldots,z^{\star}_{d})\in\mathcal{Z}=\{0,1\}^{d}, sampled uniformly from ρ0\rho_{0}. The action space is 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}, and the observation space is Ω={0,1,⊥}\Omega=\{0,1,\bot\}. The surface state is only the turn index, s⁡(ht)=ts(h_{t})=t, so a belief-agnostic policy may know the depth but not the posterior induced by observed evidence.

At turn t=0t=0, action a0=0a_{0}=0 always reveals the first latent bit: o0=z1⋆o_{0}=z^{\star}_{1}. Action a0=1a_{0}=1 returns o0=⊥o_{0}=\bot. For turns t≥1t\geq 1, the environment reveals the next latent bit if and only if the agent chooses the previously revealed bit:

ot={zt+1⋆,if ​at=zt⋆,⊥,otherwise.o_{t}=\begin{cases}z^{\star}_{t+1},&\text{if }a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t},\\ \bot,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The terminal reward is RT=1R_{T}=1 if the agent has observed all dd latent bits by the end of the episode, and RT=0R_{T}=0 otherwise. Since at most one bit is revealed per turn, any ⊥\bot observation prevents success.

The key design principle is that the correct action at turn tt is determined by the observation ot−1=zt⋆o_{t-1}=z^{\star}_{t} received at the previous turn. This observation is part of the history hth_{t} and therefore encoded in the belief btb_{t}, but it is not a function of the surface state s⁡(ht)=ts(h_{t})=t alone.

Step 2: An epistemically adaptive policy succeeds with probability one.

Define π⋆\pi^{\star} as follows. At t=0t=0, choose a0=0a_{0}=0, which reveals z1⋆z^{\star}_{1}. At each later turn t≥1t\geq 1, choose at=zt⋆a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t}, the bit revealed as observation ot−1o_{t-1} at the previous turn.

This action is accessible to π⋆\pi^{\star}: the value zt⋆=ot−1z^{\star}_{t}=o_{t-1} is contained in the history ht=(a0,o0,…,at−1,ot−1)h_{t}=(a_{0},o_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) and hence in the posterior belief btb_{t}. An epistemically adaptive policy can therefore compute at=zt⋆a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t} from btb_{t}.

By induction, after turn tt, the agent has observed z1⋆,…,zt+1⋆z^{\star}_{1},\ldots,z^{\star}_{t+1}. After d−1d-1 turns of this form, the agent has observed the full latent string z⋆z^{\star}, so ℙ⁡(success∣π⋆)=1\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\pi^{\star})=1.

Step 3: Belief-agnostic policies cannot use the revealed bit.

Let μ\mu be any belief-agnostic policy. Since s⁡(ht)=ts(h_{t})=t, the policy conditions only on the turn index: μ⁡(at∣ht)=μt​(at)\mu(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=\mu_{t}(a_{t}) for some distribution μt∈Δ⁡({0,1})\mu_{t}\in\Delta(\{0,1\}), independent of the observations received.

At t=0t=0, the best belief-agnostic policy chooses a0=0a_{0}=0, so we upper bound its probability of passing the first turn by 11.

For any later turn t≥1t\geq 1, success requires at=zt⋆a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t}. The value zt⋆z^{\star}_{t} was revealed as observation ot−1o_{t-1}, but μ\mu does not condition on ot−1o_{t-1}. Conditional on success at all previous turns—which is required for zt⋆z^{\star}_{t} to have been revealed—the revealed bit zt⋆z^{\star}_{t} is uniformly distributed on {0,1}\{0,1\} by symmetry of the prior. Therefore, for any fixed action distribution μt\mu_{t}:

ℙ⁡(at=zt⋆∣success​up​to​t−1,μ)=∑a∈{0,1}μt​(a)​ℙ​(zt⋆=a)=μt​(0)+μt​(1)2=12.\mathbb{P}(a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t}\mid\mathrm{success\ up\ to\ }t-1,\,\mu)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\mu_{t}(a)\,\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}_{t}=a)=\frac{\mu_{t}(0)+\mu_{t}(1)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.

The equality holds regardless of the mixing weights μt​(0),μt​(1)\mu_{t}(0),\mu_{t}(1) because the bit zt⋆z^{\star}_{t} is symmetric.

Step 4: Chaining the per-turn bounds.

For the terminal reward RT=1R_{T}=1, the agent must choose the correct action at every turn t=1,…,d−1t=1,\ldots,d-1 (turn t=0t=0 succeeds with probability 11 under the best belief-agnostic policy). The events {at=zt⋆}\{a_{t}=z^{\star}_{t}\} are conditionally independent across turns given the latent string z⋆z^{\star}, because μt\mu_{t} is a fixed distribution and z1⋆,…,zd⋆z^{\star}_{1},\ldots,z^{\star}_{d} are independent bits. Therefore:

ℙ⁡(success∣μ)≤1⋅∏t=1d−112=21−d.\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\mu)\leq 1\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{d-1}\frac{1}{2}=2^{1-d}.

Combined with Part 1, this gives ℙ⁡(success∣π⋆)=1\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\pi^{\star})=1 versus ℙ⁡(success∣μ)≤21−d\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{success}\mid\mu)\leq 2^{1-d} for any belief-agnostic μ\mu, establishing the claimed separation.

Remark.

This construction is related to the binary tree construction in [70] (Theorem 4.3), where an epistemically adaptive policy succeeds with probability 11 in a depth-dd tree while any Markovian policy succeeds with probability 1/2d−11/2^{d-1}. The key difference is the proof technique: their argument uses a visit-frequency induction on tree nodes under Markovian policies, while our argument uses the direct symmetry of the per-turn bit under belief-agnostic action selection. Both constructions achieve an exponential gap of 2Ω⁡(d)2^{\Omega(d)}, but ours is more direct for the EDP setting because it does not require the full tree structure—only a sequential bit-reveal chain. ∎

Theorem A.3 (Spectral aliasing of trajectory-level credit).

Fix a policy π\pi in an EDP and a turn tt. Let ω\omega denote a full sampled trajectory, let G⁡(ω)=∑s=0T−1rs​(ω)G(\omega)=\sum_{s=0}^{T-1}r_{s}(\omega) be its total return, and let

A⁡(ω)=ABπ​(ht​(ω),at​(ω))A(\omega)=A_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t}(\omega),a_{t}(\omega))

be the Bayesian advantage of the action taken at turn tt. Consider the class of trajectory-level estimators A^ttraj=ϕ⁡(G)\widehat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}=\phi(G), where ϕ\phi is any measurable function of the total return.

Let ℋ=L2​(Ω,ℙπ)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{P}_{\pi}) and let ℋG={ϕ⁡(G):ϕ∈L2}\mathcal{H}_{G}=\{\phi(G):\phi\in L^{2}\} be the closed subspace of return-measurable functions. Let ΠG:ℋ→ℋG\Pi_{G}:\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}_{G} be the orthogonal projection onto this subspace, i.e. ΠG​A=𝔼⁡[A∣G]\Pi_{G}A=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G]. Then

infϕ𝔼⁡[(ϕ⁡(G)−A)2]=‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(A∣G)].\inf_{\phi}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\phi(G)-A\right)^{2}\right]=\left\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\right\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G)\right].

Consequently, if ABπ​(ht,at)A_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t}) is not measurable with respect to the total return GG, then any trajectory-level estimator has strictly positive irreducible statewise error.

Proof.

We view advantage estimation as an approximation problem in the Hilbert space ℋ=L2​(Ω,ℙπ)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{P}_{\pi}), equipped with inner product ⟨f,g⟩=𝔼⁡[f​g]\langle f,g\rangle=\mathbb{E}[fg]. The class of trajectory-level estimators ϕ⁡(G)\phi(G) is exactly the subspace ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} of functions measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra generated by GG.

The conditional expectation ΠG​A=𝔼⁡[A∣G]\Pi_{G}A=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G] is the orthogonal projection of AA onto ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}. Therefore, for any ϕ⁡(G)∈ℋG\phi(G)\in\mathcal{H}_{G}, we have the orthogonal decomposition

ϕ⁡(G)−A=ϕ⁡(G)−ΠG​A⏟∈ℋG−(I−ΠG)​A⏟⟂ℋG.\phi(G)-A=\underbrace{\phi(G)-\Pi_{G}A}_{\in\mathcal{H}_{G}}-\underbrace{(I-\Pi_{G})A}_{\perp\mathcal{H}_{G}}.

By Pythagoras,

‖ϕ⁡(G)−A‖22=‖ϕ⁡(G)−ΠG​A‖22+‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22.\|\phi(G)-A\|_{2}^{2}=\|\phi(G)-\Pi_{G}A\|_{2}^{2}+\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}.

The first term is minimized by choosing ϕ⋆​(G)=ΠG​A=𝔼⁡[A∣G]\phi^{\star}(G)=\Pi_{G}A=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G], leaving the irreducible residual ‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}. Since conditional expectation gives the best L2L^{2} predictor, this residual is

‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22=𝔼⁡[(A−𝔼⁡[A∣G])2]=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(A∣G)].\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(A-\mathbb{E}[A\mid G]\right)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G)\right].

If AA is not measurable with respect to GG, then A≠ΠG​AA\neq\Pi_{G}A on a set of positive probability, so ‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22>0\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}>0. This proves the claim. ∎

Corollary A.4 (Finite-dimensional view of trajectory-level aliasing).

Assume the trajectory space is finite, Ω={ω1,…,ωn}\Omega=\{\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{n}\}, with probabilities pi=ℙπ​(ωi)>0p_{i}=\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\omega_{i})>0. Let Ai=A⁡(ωi)A_{i}=A(\omega_{i}), where A⁡(ω)=ABπ​(ht​(ω),at​(ω))A(\omega)=A_{\mathrm{B}}^{\pi}(h_{t}(\omega),a_{t}(\omega)), and let Gi=G⁡(ωi)G_{i}=G(\omega_{i}) be the total return of trajectory ωi\omega_{i}. Let ΠG\Pi_{G} denote the orthogonal projection onto the subspace of functions measurable with respect to GG, under the weighted inner product ⟨f,g⟩=∑i=1npi​fi​gi\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}f_{i}g_{i}. Then

(ΠG​A)i=𝔼⁡[A∣G=Gi],(\Pi_{G}A)_{i}=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G=G_{i}],

i.e., ΠG\Pi_{G} replaces each trajectory-level advantage by the average Bayesian advantage among trajectories with the same total return. Moreover, ΠG\Pi_{G} is self-adjoint and idempotent, so its spectrum is contained in {0,1}\{0,1\}. The eigenspace with eigenvalue 11 consists of functions that are constant on each return level set, while the eigenspace with eigenvalue 00 consists of within-level-set contrasts whose conditional mean given GG is zero.

Consequently, the irreducible error of any trajectory-level estimator ϕ⁡(G)\phi(G) is exactly the squared norm of the component of AA lying outside the return-measurable subspace:

infϕ‖ϕ⁡(G)−A‖22=‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22=∑gℙ⁡(G=g)​Var⁡(A∣G=g).\inf_{\phi}\|\phi(G)-A\|_{2}^{2}=\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{g}\mathbb{P}(G=g)\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G=g).

Thus, if two positive-probability trajectories have the same total return but require different Bayesian credit at turn tt, then trajectory-level estimators cannot recover that within-return difference.

Proof.

Since ΠG\Pi_{G} is the conditional expectation operator 𝔼[⋅∣G]\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid G], it maps each value AiA_{i} to the average of AA over all trajectories with the same total return GiG_{i}. Thus (ΠG​A)i=𝔼⁡[A∣G=Gi](\Pi_{G}A)_{i}=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G=G_{i}].

The operator ΠG\Pi_{G} is an orthogonal projection in L2​(Ω,ℙπ)L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{P}_{\pi}), so ΠG∗=ΠG\Pi_{G}^{\ast}=\Pi_{G} and ΠG2=ΠG\Pi_{G}^{2}=\Pi_{G}. Therefore every eigenvalue λ\lambda satisfies λ2=λ\lambda^{2}=\lambda, implying λ∈{0,1}\lambda\in\{0,1\}. The 11-eigenspace is the range of ΠG\Pi_{G}, namely the set of functions measurable with respect to GG, which are exactly the functions that are constant on each return level set. The 00-eigenspace is the nullspace of ΠG\Pi_{G}, namely functions ff satisfying 𝔼⁡[f∣G]=0\mathbb{E}[f\mid G]=0, which are precisely within-level-set contrasts.

By Theorem A.3, the best trajectory-level estimator is ΠG​A=𝔼⁡[A∣G]\Pi_{G}A=\mathbb{E}[A\mid G], and its residual is (I−ΠG)​A(I-\Pi_{G})A. Therefore

infϕ‖ϕ⁡(G)−A‖22=‖(I−ΠG)​A‖22=𝔼⁡[Var⁡(A∣G)].\inf_{\phi}\|\phi(G)-A\|_{2}^{2}=\|(I-\Pi_{G})A\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G)].

In the finite case, this conditional variance expands as

𝔼⁡[Var⁡(A∣G)]=∑gℙ⁡(G=g)​Var⁡(A∣G=g).\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G)]=\sum_{g}\mathbb{P}(G=g)\operatorname{Var}(A\mid G=g).

If AA varies among trajectories in the same return level set, then at least one conditional variance term is positive, so the residual is strictly positive. ∎

Remark A.5.

Why this matters for epistemic credit. Corollary A.4 makes the limitation of trajectory-level credit explicit. Total return partitions trajectories into return level sets, and any estimator ϕ⁡(G)\phi(G) can only assign credit that is constant within each level set. However, in an EDP, two trajectories can have the same final return while requiring different credit for an intermediate action because the action was taken under a different belief state. This within-return variation is exactly the component (I−ΠG)​A(I-\Pi_{G})A, which lies outside the return-measurable subspace and is therefore invisible to any trajectory-level estimator. The failure is not finite-sample noise or poor optimization; it is an aliasing44 4 We use the term “aliasing” by analogy to signal processing, where distinct high-frequency components can become indistinguishable under a coarse sampling operator [44, 57]. In our setting, the coarse observation is the aggregate return GG: trajectories with different belief-conditioned advantages can collapse to the same return level set. problem caused by projecting belief-dependent credit onto a coarser signal.

Connection to policy-gradient baselines. This result is complementary to classical policy-gradient variance-reduction analyses such as Greensmith et al. [21]. Those analyses study how baselines reduce variance when they condition on useful state information. Our result identifies the opposite obstruction in EDPs: if the estimator conditions only on aggregate return, then the projection subspace is too small to recover belief-dependent advantage components. In other words, the issue is not merely choosing a better scalar baseline; the estimator must expose information about the epistemic state.

Lemma A.6 (Exact posterior in CSG).

Let z⋆z^{\star} be drawn uniformly from {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} and let 𝒞0={1,…,N}\mathcal{C}_{0}=\{1,\ldots,N\}. Suppose the oracle responds truthfully at every turn, i.e., p(ot∣z⋆=z,at)=𝟏[z∈𝒞t+1]p(o_{t}\mid z^{\star}\!=\!z,\,a_{t})=\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}], where 𝒞t+1⊆𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t+1}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{t} is the set of candidates consistent with observation oto_{t}. Then for all t≥0t\geq 0, the posterior is exactly uniform over the remaining candidate set:

bt​(z)=ℙ⁡(z⋆=z∣ht)=𝟏[z∈𝒞t]|𝒞t|.b_{t}(z)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(z^{\star}=z\mid h_{t})\;=\;\frac{\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}]}{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}.
Proof.

We prove this by induction. Notice that the base case holds by construction: b0​(z)=1/N=1/|𝒞0|b_{0}(z)=1/N=1/|\mathcal{C}_{0}| for all zz.

For the inductive step, assume bt(z)=𝟏[z∈𝒞t]/|𝒞t|b_{t}(z)=\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}]/|\mathcal{C}_{t}|. After action ata_{t} and observation oto_{t}, Bayes’ rule gives

bt+1​(z)=bt​(z)​p​(ot∣z,at)∑z′bt​(z′)​p​(ot∣z′,at).b_{t+1}(z)=\frac{b_{t}(z)\;p(o_{t}\mid z,\,a_{t})}{\sum_{z^{\prime}}b_{t}(z^{\prime})\;p(o_{t}\mid z^{\prime},\,a_{t})}.

Substituting the inductive hypothesis and the binary likelihood:

bt+1​(z)=𝟏[z∈𝒞t]|𝒞t|⋅𝟏[z∈𝒞t+1]∑z′∈𝒞t1|𝒞t|⋅𝟏[z′∈𝒞t+1]=𝟏[z∈𝒞t+1]|𝒞t+1|,b_{t+1}(z)=\frac{\frac{\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}]}{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}\cdot\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}]}{\sum_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}\cdot\mathbf{1}[z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}]}=\frac{\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}]}{|\mathcal{C}_{t+1}|},

where the numerator uses 𝒞t+1⊆𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t+1}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{t}, so 𝟏[z∈𝒞t]⋅𝟏[z∈𝒞t+1]=𝟏[z∈𝒞t+1]\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}]\cdot\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}]=\mathbf{1}[z\in\mathcal{C}_{t+1}], and the denominator sums to |𝒞t+1|/|𝒞t||\mathcal{C}_{t+1}|/|\mathcal{C}_{t}|, which cancels |𝒞t||\mathcal{C}_{t}|. ∎

Remark.

The oracle in CGS is implemented via GPT-4o mini, so the observation kernel O⁡(ot∣z⋆,ht,at)O(o_{t}\mid z^{\star},h_{t},a_{t}) is stochastic55 5 https://community.openai.com/t/why-does-openai-api-behave-randomly-with-temperature-0-and-top-p-0/934104 rather than deterministic—even at temperature set to zero. However, the candidate-set update removes inconsistent candidates given the realized observation, so btb_{t} is exact conditional on oto_{t}; the stochasticity enters through the EDP environment dynamics (Section 3), not through belief-approximation error. This makes the turn reward rt=(|𝒞t|−|𝒞t+1|)/|𝒞t|r_{t}=(|\mathcal{C}_{t}|-|\mathcal{C}_{t+1}|)/|\mathcal{C}_{t}| a direct measure of posterior contraction, computable in closed form without learned reward models or Monte Carlo EIG estimation [10].

Connection to BAMDPs and epistemic planning.

EDPs are best viewed as a task-level specialization of belief-state decision processes, rather than as a representationally separate alternative to POMDPs or BAMDPs. The distinction is one of modeling focus, but one that leverages the expressivity of LLMs that naturally operate in exponentially complex language-based state-action spaces. BAMDPs typically maintain beliefs over unknown transition or reward parameters, or over latent MDP identities that are computationally expensive to track with LLMs, and use interaction to improve control under environment uncertainty. Epistemic planning methods such as Reflect-then-Plan similarly reason over model uncertainty to improve offline-to-online planning [27]. In contrast, EDPs target information-seeking language agents operating through a fixed interaction interface: the environment need not be unknown in its dynamics, but the current task variable z⋆z^{\star} is hidden (See ). The relevant belief is therefore a posterior over task hypotheses, p⁡(z⋆∣ht)p(z^{\star}\mid h_{t}), and the central question is whether an action acquires evidence that changes this posterior. Prior work [70] is closest in spirit, using Bayes-adaptive RL to induce uncertainty-adaptive reflection over reasoning chains or MDP hypotheses [70]; EDPs instead focus on external66 6 In contrast to [70], where adaptivity emerges “in-context” aka in reasoning chains within a turn, our focus in on adaptivity in an external sense i.e., across interaction turns. query actions and observable belief updates across interaction turns. Thus, the contribution of EDPs is not a new belief-state formalism in the abstract, but a lens that makes the credit signal for information-seeking actions explicit.

Appendix B ECHO Training Dynamics

Agent Prompts

Figure 6 (A) shows prompts used for training of LLM agents in CSG environment as well as evaluation. Figure 6 (B) shows the prompt used to instantiate the clue (or hint) provider model with GPT-4o-mini with near-deterministic inference with temperature (T=0T=0). The CSG uses two prompts with distinct roles. The selector prompt presents the agent with its current belief state — the remaining candidate list CtC_{t} and the full arm query history — and requires structured JSON output specifying an arm index and a property question. No chain-of-thought or reasoning scaffold is provided; the agent must select informative actions directly from the belief state encoding. The oracle prompt is given to a fixed gpt-4o-mini clue holder at temperature zero, which receives the secret number and the agent’s question and returns a single deterministic sentence answering only the queried property. The oracle is explicitly instructed not to volunteer information beyond what was asked and to deflect vague questions, enforcing strict information separation across the K=5K{=}5 arms. Repeat questions to the same arm incur a penalty of rt=−0.1r_{t}=-0.1 rather than an oracle call, discouraging redundant queries. This design ensures that all information gain flows exclusively through the structured arm–question interface, making the per-turn reward signal a clean measure of epistemic progress.

Training dynamics and mechanism analysis.

Figure 7 along with main metrics in Figure 5 (Section 6) decomposes training into outcome, mechanism, and optimization-health metrics. The main pattern is that ECHO improves not only final task success, but also the intermediate epistemic behavior predicted by the EDP analysis. Episode resolve rate rises sharply, while mean eliminated candidates per turn increases, indicating that the policy learns to ask questions that contract the current candidate set more effectively. At the same time, redundancy falls to near zero, showing that the policy is not simply repeating high-probability questions, but is using the evolving history to avoid already-exhausted information. This supports the central motivation for turn-level epistemic credit: when the reward signal is assigned at the decision depth where an action changes the posterior, the policy receives direct supervision about which questions are useful under the current belief state.

Specialization without collapse.

The diagnostic metrics further suggest that ECHO’s gains reflect healthy specialization rather than mode collapse. Entropy decreases during training, showing that the policy becomes more decisive, but diversity remains near saturation, indicating that it does not collapse onto a small set of repeated questions. Mechanistically, the policy appears to learn strong within-step information gathering before fully mastering higher-level arm selection: candidate elimination and efficiency improve substantially, while arm-match remains comparatively weaker. This is consistent with the task structure, where the policy must learn a joint action consisting of both an arm choice and a natural-language question. In EDP terms, ECHO first improves posterior-sensitive local action quality—asking useful questions for the current candidate set—while leaving additional headroom for learning better long-horizon coordination over which information source to query.

Seed-level significance.

We compute final-window means over the last 100 training steps for each seed and compare ECHO against episodic GRPO using paired seed-level tests. Table 2 shows the results. Across all three seeds, ECHO improves the primary outcome and mechanism metrics: episode resolve rate increases from 17.1%17.1\% to 66.1%66.1\%, mean eliminated candidates rises from 10.5410.54 to 12.9212.92, turn resolve rate increases from 1.94%1.94\% to 8.66%8.66\%, and mean episode length decreases from 9.149.14 to 7.727.72. Paired tt-tests are significant for these metrics despite the small number of seeds, reflecting consistent improvements across runs. Since n=3n=3, we interpret these results primarily through effect size and cross-seed consistency rather than relying solely on significance tests.

Appendix C Additional Results

C.1 Main Evaluation Metric Definitions

We compute task-level and process-level metrics from CSG episode logs over 10 maximum turns. Unless otherwise stated, turn-level metrics are averaged over turns within a run, and model-level values report mean and standard error across runs. Additional metrics that we consider and those that CSG RL training environment provides are noted in Table 10 (for training-related metrics) and Table 4 (for arm-routing specific metrics).

  • •

    Resolve measures final task success: the fraction of episodes in which the agent identifies the secret within the turn budget.

  • •

    Zero measures zero-elimination behavior: the fraction of non-redundant turns that eliminate no candidates from the current candidate set. Redundant turns are excluded so that Zero captures new but uninformative questions.

  • •

    Qual. measures candidate-elimination quality relative to the current belief state. It normalizes the number of eliminated candidates by an ideal binary split of the current candidate set and caps the value at 11. Thus, high Qual. indicates questions that efficiently partition the remaining candidate set.

  • •

    Ground measures grounded information seeking: the fraction of turns that are both non-redundant and sufficiently informative under the current candidate set. In our implementation, a turn is grounded when its elimination quality is at least 0.50.5.

  • •

    LateCalib measures late-stage redundancy in narrow belief states. It is computed on turns with small remaining candidate sets late in the episode and records whether the action was redundant. Lower values indicate fewer wasted turns after the belief state has already narrowed.

  • •

    Reason% measures visible reasoning text outside the required structured action format. It is used only as a diagnostic for whether a policy relies on explicit natural-language rationales rather than direct action selection.

  • •

    ZeroEvents counts zero-elimination non-redundant turns that have a following turn, and serves as the event denominator for recovery metrics.

  • •

    Rec1 measures weak immediate recovery after a Zero event: the fraction of Zero events after which the next turn is non-redundant and eliminates at least one candidate. It captures whether the agent resumes gaining any information at all.

  • •

    GRecover measures grounded immediate recovery after a Zero event: the fraction of Zero events after which the next turn is grounded, meaning non-redundant and sufficiently informative under the current candidate set. This is stricter than Rec1 because the next turn must not merely eliminate something; it must pass the groundedness threshold.

  • •

    RecQ measures the elimination quality of the immediate next turn after a Zero event.

  • •

    NextZero measures whether a Zero event is followed by another zero-elimination non-redundant turn. Lower is better.

  • •

    NextBad measures whether a Zero event is followed by either another Zero event or a redundant turn. Lower is better.

  • •

    TTR measures the number of turns until the next grounded turn after a Zero event, averaged over cases where grounded recovery occurs. Lower is better.

  • •

    TTRsucc measures whether a grounded recovery occurs at any later turn after a Zero event before the episode ends.

  • •

    ResAfterZero measures episode-level robustness after local failure: among episodes containing at least one Zero event, it reports the fraction that still resolve.

C.2 From Credit Signal to Strategy: The Emergence of Binary Search

Oracle response distributions reveal emergent strategy.

To characterize policy behavior beyond resolve rate, we analyze the distribution of oracle hint types received across evaluation episodes in CSG. This is shown in Table 3. For each turn, we classify the oracle response into coarse categories such as range, parity, divisibility, primality, square, digit properties, between, uninformative, and redundant, using keyword matching against the hint string. We also report the zero-elimination rate: the fraction of non-redundant turns where the selected question eliminated no candidates. This captures cases where the agent asked a valid question, but the question was unhelpful under the current belief state. Table 3 shows that ECHO has the lowest zero-elimination rate among evaluated policies (18.6%18.6\%), substantially below trajectory-level GRPO (Episodic Return) (39.8%39.8\%), RLOO per-turn (40.2%40.2\%), and prompting baselines such as Qwen2.5-1.5B + CoT (38.4%38.4\%) and full ReAct (49.2%49.2\%). Its hint distribution is also highly concentrated on range-based clues (60.7%60.7\%), with low redundancy (0.6%0.6\%) and little reliance on digit-property or miscellaneous hints. This suggests that ECHO does not merely improve final resolution; it changes the mechanism of interaction toward consistently informative, belief-sensitive queries.

Bisection as a special case of the EDP objective.

The emergence of binary search in ECHO is a consequence of the CSG environment, not a universal property of epistemically adaptive policies. In CSG, the initial prior is uniform, ρ0=Unif⁡({1,…,N})\rho_{0}=\mathrm{Unif}(\{1,\ldots,N\}), and deterministic oracle filtering preserves a uniform posterior over the remaining candidates, bt=Unif⁡(𝒞t)b_{t}=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{C}_{t}). For a binary question that partitions 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} into fractions pp and 1−p1-p, the expected fractional elimination is

𝔼z⋆∼bt​[u⁡(bt,at,ot)]=2​p​(1−p),\mathbb{E}_{z^{\star}\sim b_{t}}[u(b_{t},a_{t},o_{t})]=2p(1-p),

which is maximized at p=1/2p=1/2. Thus, under uniform beliefs, deterministic binary observations, and equal action costs, the EDP objective recovers bisection as the information-theoretically optimal strategy.

In general EDPs, these conditions need not hold. If the belief is non-uniform, as in diagnosis or retrieval settings, the optimal query should account for posterior mass rather than split the hypothesis set evenly. If observations are graded, noisy, or multi-valued, the optimal action depends on the task-specific observation model and belief geometry. The Bayesian value QBπ​(ht,at)=𝔼z⋆∼bt​[Qπ​(ht,at∣z⋆)]Q^{\pi}_{\mathrm{B}}(h_{t},a_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{z^{\star}\sim b_{t}}[Q^{\pi}(h_{t},a_{t}\mid z^{\star})] remains the relevant object, but its maximizer is not necessarily a bisection question. Thus, bisection is a special solution for the uniform-prior, deterministic-observation regime of CSGG, while the EDP framework and ECHO’s posterior-sensitive turn-level credit are more general.

Binary-search-like strategy in CSG

In our experiments in CSG, the hint distribution clearly explains why ECHO converges toward a binary-search-like strategy rather than the digit-property-heavy strategy used by the greedy oracle. In the CSG instantiation of the EDP (Section 5), the dominant evidential utility is fractional candidate elimination, u⁡(bt,at,ot)=|𝒞t∖𝒞t+1|/|𝒞t|u(b_{t},a_{t},o_{t})=|\mathcal{C}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{t+1}|/|\mathcal{C}_{t}|, which measures posterior contraction relative to the current belief size. Since the secret is sampled uniformly and oracle observations only eliminate inconsistent candidates, bt=Unif⁡(𝒞t)b_{t}=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{C}_{t}). For a binary question whose “yes” set occupies fraction pp of the current candidate set, the expected fractional elimination under this uniform belief is 2​p​(1−p)2p(1-p), maximized at p=1/2p=1/2. Range-bisection questions can therefore achieve near-maximal expected utility by splitting 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} roughly in half. By contrast, digit-property questions such as last digit or digit sum can be highly discriminative for some secrets, but often correspond to imbalanced predicates under the uniform posterior, giving lower expected utility on average. Thus, ECHO learns the policy that is optimal for an agent uncertain over z⋆z^{\star}: ask questions that maximize expected posterior collapse. The greedy oracle baseline, in contrast, effectively conditions on the true latent variable and can exploit digit properties with high realized elimination for that specific secret, explaining its 50.7%50.7\% combined use of last-digit and digit-sum hints versus ECHO’s 60.7%60.7\% use of range clues.

Arm routing versus belief-conditioned information seeking.

Table 5 tests whether ECHO’s gains are explained by raw arm exploration, static arm matching, or belief-conditioned information gain. The results rule out a simple exploration account: ECHO has lower arm entropy than several weaker baselines such as GRPO, RLOO, and Qwen2.5-1.5B base model, yet achieves substantially higher resolve rate. Instead, ECHO exhibits the strongest learned-policy combination of low zero-elimination rate, high elimination quality, high groundedness, and high semantic compatibility between selected arms and question types. Raw ArmMatch alone is not sufficient to explain performance: ECHO’s ArmMatch is modest, but its selected arm-question pairs eliminate candidates much more reliably than GRPO or base-model baselines. The same-arm diagnostics further show that arm repetition is not inherently harmful. While frontier models often suffer when reusing an arm, ECHO’s same-arm turns remain highly informative, with lower zero-elimination and higher elimination quality than its switched-arm turns. This suggests that ECHO learns to reuse and route arms in a belief-conditioned manner rather than merely maximizing static arm labels.

C.3 RL Results

CSG Reward Composition

The reward rtr_{t} is computed as follows. See Section 5 for motivation on why this reward design is appropriate for our theoretical and experimental setup. Specifically, if the policy has already asked the same question to the selected arm earlier in the episode, the turn returns immediately with the redundancy penalty rt=−0.1r_{t}=-0.1 and the oracle is not consulted. Otherwise the oracle returns a hint, the candidate set is filtered, and rtr_{t} is the sum of up to five components: the fractional information gain rinfo=(candidates_before−candidates_after)/candidates_beforer_{\text{info}}=(\text{candidates\_before}-\text{candidates\_after})/\text{candidates\_before}, which lies in [0,1][0,1] and dominates the dense per-turn signal; an arm-match bonus of +0.05+0.05 when the question matches a property the selected arm covers (keyword match against ARM_PROPERTIES); a diversity bonus of +0.05+0.05 when the question has not been asked to any arm earlier in the episode; a sparse resolution bonus of +1.0+1.0 when the post-oracle candidate set equals {secret}\{\text{secret}\}; and an efficiency bonus of 0.1⋅(Tmax−t)0.1\cdot(T_{\max}-t) on resolution, with Tmax=10T_{\max}=10 turns.

Training Hyperparameters

The KL coefficient is set to βKL=0\beta_{\text{KL}}=0 to remove the reference-model anchor and permit policy drift during the continuation phase; gradients are clipped at ‖∇‖≤0.5\|\nabla\|\leq 0.5; the PPO clip range uses the TRL default. The information-gain term dominates over most of training (range [0,1][0,1] per turn vs. ≤0.1\leq 0.1 for the shaping bonuses), making per-turn elimination the primary gradient signal. The resolution bonus is sparse but large at +1.0+1.0 once per resolved episode, supplying the long-horizon reward needed to escape the local optimum of asking individually informative questions that fail to fully resolve. The redundancy penalty acts as a hard early-return: in the pre-fix regime the policy frequently selected duplicate (arm, question) pairs, triggering the penalty on a large fraction of turns and short-circuiting all other reward components, so the gradient saw −0.1-0.1 rather than the information-gain landscape underneath. Setting βKL=0\beta_{\text{KL}}=0 removes the reference-model anchor, trading trajectory-drift risk for faster specialization during the continuation phase.
